chunks: My father, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and Ali ibn al-Husayn all narrated to me from Sa'd ibn Abdillah ibn Abi Khalaf, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abdillah ibn al-Mughirah, from al-Husayn ibn Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Muhammad ibn Aslam al-Jabali, from Muhammad ibn Sulayman, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who performed the Hajj of Islam (obligatory Hajj), entering with Tamattu' (combining 'Umrah and Hajj). Allah helped him complete his Hajj and 'Umrah. Then he went to Madinah and said Salam to the Messenger of Allah. Then he came to you, acknowledging your right, knowing that you are Allah's proof upon His creation and the door through which one is led, and said Salam to you. Then he went to Abu Abdillah al-Husayn (peace be upon him) and said Salam to him. Then he went to Baghdad and said Salam to Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him). Then he returned to his country. When the time for Hajj came, Allah granted him what he needed to perform Hajj. Which is better for this man who has performed the Hajj of Islam: to return and perform Hajj again, or to go to Khurasan to your father, Ali ibn Musa al-Rida (peace be upon him), and say Salam to him? He (peace be upon him) said: Rather, it is better to go to Khurasan and say Salam to Abu al-Hasan. And let that be in the month of Rajab. But it is not appropriate for them to do this now, for there is fear for us and for you from the Sultan, and it angers him.
ai.seo_question: Is Ziyarah of the Imam superior to repeating the obligatory Hajj?
ai.summary: Imam al-Ja'far al-Sadiq (a.s.) establishes the superiority of Ziyarah to the living Imam over repeating the obligatory Hajj, highlighting the spiritual hierarchy of visiting the 'Hujjah of Allah' on earth. He specifically recommends performing this visit in Rajab, a month of significance in Shia tradition, while noting that political constraints ('fear of the Sultan') currently deter public practice. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on the Imam's living presence as a conduit for divine grace, elevating personal spiritual connection above ritual repetition.
